ledger.label: Ledger
ledger.description: Precision and density for ops-heavy businesses — wholesale, distribution, accounting. A light, navy-tinted canvas built for tables.

hearth.label: Hearth
hearth.description: Warmth and clarity for client-facing service businesses — salons, retail, service companies. A sage-tinted canvas built for a handful of large things.

blueprint.label: Blueprint
blueprint.description: A drafted, technical register for contractors and field-service SMEs — site management, scheduling, materials. A cooler, higher-contrast canvas.

stamp.label: Stamp
stamp.description: Looks like the POS and accounting software they already run: a solid accent band across every table header with white type in it.

swiss.label: Swiss
swiss.description: International Typographic Style: a strict grid, generous white space, black and white with a single red used only where something must be found. Every corner square; hierarchy from type scale and spacing, not decoration.

soft.label: Soft
soft.description: Cards are the same colour as the page and are lifted by a pair of light and dark shadows instead of a border. Large radii, pill buttons. For trades whose customers choose on feel.

brut.label: Brut
brut.description: The one with weight. 3px solid black borders, a hard offset shadow with no blur — like a second impression stamped on — type up to 900, and hot pink for the accent. For businesses whose customers are young and whose competition is an Instagram page. A 40-year-old trading company would look like it was joking.

ink.label: Ink
ink.description: The spacious one. A sheet of Xuan paper, ink for the words, one vermilion seal. 40px padding and 76px rows — half again looser than anything else here, so there is less on the page and every piece stands apart. Serif, square corners, no shadow. The only register in the set drawn from a Chinese brief: for a long-established shop, a tea merchant, a TCM clinic, a calligrapher — a business that sells trust rather than noise. A high-volume business will find it shows too few rows at a time.

glass.label: Glass
glass.description: The one you can see through. Cards are white at 55% and genuinely blur what is behind them, over a ground of three soft colour fields — so what you see is not a card but a pane resting on paper. It is the first register here that is not a flat rectangle: the twelve before it had only colour, radius, border and typeface to work with, and this one uses blur. For businesses that sell how something looks — design, photography, events, fitness, beauty. Wrong for a business staring at rows of paperwork for eight hours.

night.label: Night
night.description: The one with the lights off. A near-black page, cards a step lighter than it, borders at 8% white, and one orange accent that reads as lit rather than painted. Across the other thirteen registers canvas luminance ran 0.82 to 0.97 — every page this product could build was a white page. This is the first that is not. For workshops, studios, gyms, bars, events, print shops: trades whose customers judge them on how things look. Wrong for paperwork that gets printed and signed.

signboard.label: Signboard
signboard.description: A shoplot sign and the price list beneath it. The name is set in a heavy condensed face at 46px with the tracking pulled in; everything under it is a plain 15px sans. It is the first of seventeen registers whose headings use a different face from its body — every one before it declared a single family, so a page heading and a table cell looked the same. The contrast is the register, not the colour. For F&B, retail, shopfronts, events, gyms: businesses whose customers see them in passing.

lacquer.label: Lacquer
lacquer.description: A coloured ground. The page is deep oxblood, the panels are ivory and float on it, and gold is only ever a line. Measured: across the other seventeen registers, surface saturation ran 0.00 to 0.19 while accents ran 0.11 to 1.00 — colour had only ever been allowed on the smallest thing on screen. This is the first register where the page carries it. The panels stay pale on purpose: the surface the text sits on never changes contrast, which is what makes it usable for a working day. For restaurants, tea houses, bakeries, gold and jewellery, wedding and temple supply.

code.label: Code
code.description: Every character the same width. Part numbers, barcodes, quantities and job numbers line up without anybody formatting them. Measured: the other eighteen registers use nine body faces and every one is proportional — monospace changes the texture of a screen more completely than any colour does. For spare parts, phone and computer repair, printing, courier and logistics: trades whose day is codes. Not for long prose. The CJK half needs no second font — 黑体 is already fixed-width for Han characters.

tile.label: Tile
tile.description: A patterned floor. The four-petal figure and corner dots of the Peranakan tiles in every old kopitiam and shophouse in Malacca and Penang, on a cement-coloured ground. Measured: --canvas-image had been set by exactly two registers and both were gradient washes — this is the first with a repeating figure. The pattern is on the GROUND; every card is flat cream, so the contrast where the words are never changes. For kopitiam, bakeries, kaya toast, heritage cafés, herbal shops and tea merchants: businesses whose premises already have this floor.

pop.label: Pop
pop.description: The sticker one. 26px corners with a 2px pure-black edge, and a hard offset shadow rather than a blur. Three saturated colours at once — indigo, teal, amber — colour as decoration, not only as meaning. Every one of the other twenty-one registers has a single accent. For businesses whose customer chooses with their eyes and is under forty.

console.label: Console
console.description: A wall of numbers. White sidebar, slate ground, 4px corners, tiles in rows. Measured against the other sixteen: nine put a dark column on the left, four a bar across the top, and the three that stay light are typographic registers with no fill anywhere — a light sidebar with a tinted active row appeared nowhere. For an owner who opens the system to read counts.

counter.label: Counter
counter.description: Deep navy chrome, grey ground, 2px corners, no shadow anywhere, and the active row filled solid. This is the shape of the software these businesses have already used — and the densest register in the set: 34px rows, 13px body. For a day that is a list: wholesalers, dealer networks, workshops, parts shops.

contract.heading: Why these aren't just three color swaps
contract.intro: Every page built with this design system, in any of the five styles, follows the same generation contract.
pageRules: The page states its answer. The one question the page exists to answer is the largest thing on it.
States are designed, not defaulted. Before data exists, the entry form is the page. After it exists, the input collapses to a summary with a Change affordance.
Explanation sits beside the thing it explains, never a permanent banner above everything.
Actions are named for what they do, and the label matches the heading above it.
Detail folds away. Supporting evidence opens automatically only when the verdict says something is wrong.
layoutRules: Full width, left-aligned, like every other page — a centred narrow column just leaves a dead right-hand gutter.
Rows of cards don't stretch. Where two cards of different natural heights sit side by side, the shorter one doesn't grow to match.
componentRules: Weight ceiling: nothing exceeds semibold. No 700/800/900 weights, anywhere.
Tracking scales negatively with size — a large heading needs tighter tracking than body text.
Every control has a real associated label — never a placeholder standing in for one.
Numeric columns get tabular figures. Never running prose.
Status is never colour alone — every status colour is paired with a text label.
Disabled means a real disabled attribute, not faded opacity on a non-interactive element.

today.noNudges: Nothing to look at right now.
today.tellNotLogged: WhatsApp opened, but we could not note it down here.
today.missedLessons: {n, plural, one {# lesson missed} other {# lessons missed}}
today.sessionsLeft: {n, plural, one {# session left} other {# sessions left}}
today.visitsEvery: {n, plural, one {# visit} other {# visits}}, usually every {m, plural, one {# day} other {# days}}
today.saveFailed: Could not do that. Try again.
today.kind_absent_twice: Missed two lessons in a row
today.saidNothing: Nothing has been sent to anyone yet.
today.sayToCustomers: The system may write to my customers
today.sayNotYet: Switch one off and the system can no longer line up messages for them. Nothing goes out on its own yet — that needs a WhatsApp number — and anything you send from WhatsApp yourself is still listed above.

vehicles.title: Vehicles
vehicles.lede: Type a plate and see when that car was last in, what was done, and at what mileage.
vehicles.notFound: No car with that plate yet. A car joins this list when you put the plate on a job.
vehicles.failed: Could not read that. Try again.
vehicles.empty: No cars yet. Type a plate above -- if it is not there, you register it right then.
vehicles.overdueLede: Sorted by how long since they were last in. Not by mileage -- we do not know what a car reads today.
vehicles.monthsAgo: {n, plural, one {# month ago} other {# months ago}}
vehicles.everyKmHint: Leave it empty if you do not work to a fixed interval.

serials.title: Serial numbers
serials.lede: Type a chassis number, an IMEI, a SIM number -- and see where that one unit is and everything that happened to it.
serials.notFound: No unit with that number yet. Register it here and it joins the shelf.
serials.noMoves: Registered, but it has not moved yet.
serials.noneTracked: No item is tracked one by one yet. Turn one on below, then register units against it.
serials.trackedLede: A car, a fridge, a phone -- each unit has its own number and its own cost. A bag of cement does not, which is why this is off unless you turn it on.
serials.turnOnLede: Turning it on needs the shelf at zero for that item, or every unit already given a number -- otherwise the page would say 5 in stock and 0 with numbers at the same time.
serials.noneOn: Nothing is tracked one by one yet.

contracts.title: Service contracts
contracts.liveLede: The ones still running. Change how often, or stop one.
contracts.stopContractNote: Stopping it means no more visits get scheduled. The ones already done stay on the books.
contracts.lede: Who is due a visit, and which contracts are running out.
contracts.roundLede: Tick each one off at the door. Ticking it can open the job for you.
contracts.roundNone: Nothing due in this window. Sign a contract below and the dates work themselves out.
contracts.endingLede: A contract that runs out with nobody calling is a customer walking away quietly.
contracts.makeJob: Ticking Came also opens a job in
contracts.newLede: How often, starting when. The dates after that work themselves out — nothing to keep up to date.
contracts.endsOnHint: Leave Until empty for a contract that keeps running. Money is nowhere on this page on purpose — anyone who works here can see who is due, and nobody should learn the price from a round sheet.
contracts.noCustomers: Add a customer first — a contract belongs to somebody.
contracts.failed: Could not save that. Try again.

payroll.title: Pay
payroll.lede: What each person takes home, and what it costs you.
payroll.runLede: Add what they earned. What the law takes is worked out from the current tables — you do not type it.
payroll.noRun: No run open. Pick the period and open one.
payroll.noStaff: Add your people to the staff list first.
payroll.noTerms: Nobody has a rate yet. Set one below, then open the run.
payroll.failed: Could not save that. Try again.
payroll.payHint: Paying it out records the money going and locks the run — the money has reached them, so changing the sheet afterwards would not bring it back.
payroll.discardHint: Throwing it away is only possible before it is paid.
payroll.termsLede: Changes once or twice a year, so it sits at the bottom.
payroll.byLaw: worked out from the current tables
payroll.noLaw: Nobody has checked the EPF and SOCSO tables into this system yet, so these slips carry no statutory deductions. That is ours to do, not yours — tell us and we will load them.

tax.title: Tax
tax.lede: Who this business is to the tax office, what SST you collected, and what a document is still missing.
tax.whoLede: This is the top half of every e-Invoice. Fill it once.
tax.failed: Could not save that. Try again.
tax.sstLede: Leave the number empty if you are not registered — then no document shows a tax line at all.
tax.notRegistered: Not registered, so nothing charges tax. That is right for most small businesses — you only register once you go over RM 500,000 a year.
tax.checkLede: Pick a job and see exactly what is still missing before it could go to the tax office.
tax.notSent: Nothing here is sent anywhere. Sending to LHDN needs a registered company, a certificate from them and a signing key — none of which exist yet, so we do not pretend the line is connected.

expiry.title: Shelf life
expiry.lede: What is about to expire, and which batch is on the shelf.
expiry.soonLede: Oldest first. Anything already past its date is the first thing to take off the shelf.
expiry.soonNone: Nothing expiring in the next 90 days.
expiry.batchesLede: Record the batch when the goods arrive. How many are left is counted from the movements — there is no box here to type it into.
expiry.noItems: Add an item to your shelf first.
expiry.failed: Could not save that. Try again.
expiry.needCode: This batch needs its number — without it nobody can tell it apart.
expiry.noBatches: No batches on this item yet.

rentals.title: Out on loan
rentals.lede: What is out, who has it, and when it is due back.
rentals.outLede: Overdue first. Whether to charge for the late days is your call, not a formula.
rentals.lendLede: It goes out against a job, so the job answers who has it — this page does not write the name down a second time.
rentals.noJobs: Open an order or a job first — something goes out against one.
rentals.failed: Could not save that. Try again.
rentals.depositNote: The deposit is not here. Money taken and not yet applied to a job is the deposit, and it lives on the money side — so anyone who works here can see what is out without seeing what it is worth.

payables.title: What you owe
payables.lede: Suppliers you still owe, and the orders that do not add up. Worked out from the orders and the payments — nothing here is typed.
payables.none: You do not owe any supplier right now.
payables.rowNote: {docs, plural, one {# order} other {# orders}} · ordered {ordered} · paid {paid}
payables.oldest: oldest is {n, plural, one {# day} other {# days}}
payables.note: Counted from the day each order was written, not from a due date — a purchase order's date is when the goods were expected, not when the money is.
payables.pillOldest: oldest {n, plural, one {# day} other {# days}}
payables.pillBad: {n, plural, one {# does not add up} other {# do not add up}}

attendance.title: Days worked
attendance.lede: Who was on site, day by day. A day here is what the pay run counts — a half day counts as half.
attendance.noStaff: Add someone to your people list first, then their days show up here.
attendance.pickDay: Pick a day to record it.
attendance.notYet: That day has not happened yet.
attendance.saveFailed: That did not save. The day is back to what it was.
attendance.summary: {days, plural, one {# day worked} other {# days worked}} · {logged} recorded
attendance.note: A half day counts as half. Hours are only for people paid by the hour — leave it blank and nothing is recorded.

rota.title: Who is free
rota.lede: Ask for a day and a time, and see who is on and who is already taken.
rota.noStaff: Add someone to your people list first, then their hours show up here.
rota.noneRostered: Nobody has hours set yet, so everyone counts as on. Set them below and this answers properly.
rota.rosterLede: The shape of one week. Set it once — it holds until you change it. A day off, or someone away, is a blocked slot in bookings, not a second table here.
rota.rosterNote: Leave both boxes empty for a day off. A shift has to end after it starts.

transfers.title: Moving stock
transfers.lede: Send goods from one shop to another. One press writes both halves, so they cannot disagree.
transfers.needTwo: You only have one shop open, so there is nowhere to move stock to. Open a second one first.
transfers.shortWarn: Moved, and that shop was %n short.
transfers.formNote: If the shop does not have enough, it still moves and says how short it was — the goods really did leave, and it is the number that is wrong.

counter.title: Counter
counter.lede: Scan, take the money, tell them the change. One press writes the sale, takes it off the shelf and records the money.
counter.needShelf: Nothing on your shelf yet, so there is nothing to scan.
counter.needPage: This system has no page a counter sale can go on. Add an orders page first.
counter.scanNone: Nothing on the shelf has the code “{code}”.
counter.scanSerial: “{name}” is tracked one unit at a time, so it cannot go through the counter — sell it from its own job so the serial is on the document.
counter.scanFailed: That did not go through. Try scanning it again.
counter.shortShelf: The shelf was short on {n} of them — the goods left anyway.
counter.empty: Scan something to start a sale.

classes.title: Classes
classes.closeGroupNote: Closing it takes it off this page. The lessons it has already run, and who came to them, stay on the books.
classes.lede: One teacher, a room of students. Lessons for the next two weeks, and who is on each class.
classes.noneDue: No lessons in the next two weeks. Set the hours on a class below and they appear here.
classes.noGroups: No classes yet. Add one below.
classes.name: Name
classes.slotsNote: Leave both empty for a day it does not run.

process.title: Three steps between here and a system you actually use.
process.s1d: What you use to track customers today, where your time actually goes, and what happens when a new customer arrives.
process.s1n: About 2 minutes. No signup, no card.
process.s2d: Not a report — a working interface you can click and edit. Page names, table columns, workflow stages: all changed into your own words.
process.s2n: Or just type what you want changed: “rename ‘customer’ to ‘patient’”.
process.s3: We build exactly what you designed
process.s3d: A real team takes over and builds a system that issues real quotes, takes real payments and holds real records — not a prototype.
process.s3n: Typically 3 to 6 weeks, depending on scope.
process.s2c: your portal — the editor, on your own dashboard
process.s3c: your public site — what a stranger sees

scope.title: What you end up holding.
scope.d1: A system shaped like your business
scope.d1d: Not a generic template with your company name on it. Every page and every field is one you settled during the design step.
scope.d2d: Every page, every field, every stage of the workflow, written down. Take it to any development shop and they will understand it.
scope.d3d: Export all of it, any time. If you ever want someone else to run it, you leave with the data.
scope.ctaNote: Two minutes to see your own system

price.title: The price is on this page, not behind a form.

steps.label: Step one · the build
steps.note: Once. Everything you designed, built for real.
includes: your public site, with enquiries landing in the system

steps.label: After · every year
includes: export your data free, any time

price.free: Designing it costs nothing. Build the whole system, see exactly what it looks like, and only then decide whether to go ahead.

faq.title: What you are probably wondering.
faq.q1: How is this different from hiring a web shop?
faq.q1a: They start by guessing from what you described, then rebuild when it is wrong. Here you design the system first and we build that. Changing a design is free; changing code is not.
faq.q2: I am not good with computers. Can I do this?
faq.q2a: The system drafts itself from your trade first, so you are editing words, not drawing screens. If you would rather not touch it at all, type one sentence and it edits itself.
faq.q3a: The design appears in minutes. The build depends on scope — usually 3 to 6 weeks.
faq.q4: Is the data mine? Can I get locked in?
faq.q4a: It is yours, exportable in full at any time. If you want to buy the system outright and host it yourself, that is a conversation we will have.
faq.q5: Can I look before I commit?
faq.q5a: Yes. The design step costs nothing and asks for no card. If it is not for you, walk away.

footer.waMessage: Hi, I saw Formae online and would like to know more.

system.notFoundBody: The link may be wrong, or the page may have been deleted.
system.errorBody: Your data is fine — this page just failed to render. Trying again usually works.

legal.disclaimer: These were written by the people who built the system and describe what it actually does. They are not a lawyer's template. Before a real launch, have a Malaysian lawyer read them. Anything unclear, just ask us.

cookie.label: Cookie notice
cookie.body: We use one kind of cookie: the one that keeps you signed in. No ad tracking, no third-party analytics.

privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.intro: In short: we collect information about your business in order to design your system. We do not sell it, we do not advertise with it, and you can download all of it or delete all of it at any time.

sections.heading: What we collect
sections.body:
From the questionnaire: your trade, how you work today, where things get stuck.
At signup: your email and password (the password is hashed — we cannot read it).
While you use it: what you call your business, the pages you design, the style you pick.
If you use Google: the email and name Google gives us.

sections.heading: What we use it for
sections.body:
To analyse your business with AI and generate a first version of your system.
To let you sign in, save, and come back to it.
To build the real system from your design when you ask us to.
Those three things. Nothing else.

sections.heading: Where it lives
sections.body:
In Supabase (Postgres), on servers in Singapore (ap-southeast-1).
The site runs on Vercel.
What you type into the AI assistant is sent to OpenAI to process, and is not used for training.
No fourth party.

sections.heading: Who can see it
sections.body:
You.
And Formae's founder — he has to see what you designed in order to build it. That is the service.
No other customer can see yours. That is enforced in the database itself (Row Level Security), not by application code remembering to check.

sections.heading: How long we keep it
sections.body:
As long as your account exists.
Delete your account and your account, system, pages and history are permanently deleted.
The questionnaire record is kept (it no longer carries your identity once the account is gone) because it is our own business record.

sections.heading: What you can do
sections.body:
Download everything any time (My account → Export my data, JSON, free).
Delete your account any time (My account → Delete account).
Change your email or password on the same page.
Ask us anything on WhatsApp.

terms.title: Terms of service
terms.intro: What each of us is responsible for. Designing is free and you can change it as often as you like; you pay when you decide to have it built.

sections.heading: What this service is
sections.body:
You use Formae to design the business system you want — which pages, what goes on each, what the columns are called, how the workflow runs.
Then our team builds a real, working system from that design.
Formae itself is not that system. It is where you design and approve it.

sections.heading: Fees
sections.body:
Designing: free. Change it as often as you like, and saving is free too.
Build: RM 1,500, once — sign-in, roles, the shell, your public site and every page you designed.
Every year after: RM 1,500 — hosting and your public site.
Payment is by bank transfer. There is no online payment yet.

sections.heading: Your work is yours
sections.body:
The system you design and the data you put in it are yours.
You can export all of it at any time, free.
If you later want to own the whole system outright (code and database), that is a separate conversation and a separate fee.

sections.heading: What we are responsible for
sections.body:
We will build what you approved.
We do not promise the system will make you more money — that depends on how you use it.
While you are hosted with us, we keep it running. Stop hosting and it stops.
If we lose your data through our own fault, we restore it. What you delete yourself, we cannot.

sections.heading: When we would close an account
sections.body:
Using it for something illegal.
Using it to attack this system or anyone else's.
Hosting unpaid for a long time.
Otherwise we will not close your account. If we ever have to, we tell you first and give you time to export.

sections.heading: Changes
sections.body:
If these terms change we will tell you at your next sign-in.
Price increases are not retroactive — a price already agreed is the price.

showroom.heading: This is the system that sentence produced.
showroom.body: Five pages, four tables, seventeen fields — in your trade’s own words, with your workflow, and every part of it editable. Not a screenshot: the actual thing you get.
showroom.rule: FROM HERE DOWN, IT IS YOURS

receipt.title: What you walk away with.
receipt.body: Not a proposal. A document that names every page, every table and every field — you read it before you decide anything.
receipt.freeV: free, as often as you like

drawing.title: One sentence, drawn into a system.
drawing.body: <m>Nothing here is a picture.</m> The frame, the rail, the tiles, the table and the workflow are drawn line by line as you read — the same order the generator builds them in.
drawing.alt: A wireframe of a system being drawn: outer frame, sidebar, four figures, a record table, a workflow strip.
drawing.s3: the four figures you check first
drawing.s6: where a job is right now
drawing.aside: the order you are watching is the order the generator really builds in

draw1.title: Two minutes of your own words.
draw1.body: No form, no checkboxes. You describe the business the way you would describe it to a friend, and <m>every noun in it becomes something the system has to hold</m>.
draw1.s2: broken into what you actually said
draw1.s3: the trade and the verbs it recognises
draw1.s4: the modules that follow from them
draw1.aside: these three drawings are inline vectors — 0 requests, 0 photographs, and they still print

draw3.title: You hand it over. It starts working.
draw3.body: The specification goes to a real team, the system gets built, and the public site goes up with it — so <m>a stranger filling in the form lands as a row in the system you designed</m>.
draw3.s4: a stranger asks for a price
draw3.s5: it lands as a record, in your columns
draw3.aside: that arrow is live today: an enquiry from the public site becomes a record, with no copy-paste
